♻ ☆ PRIMA: Preference-Informed Multimodal Trajectory Planning with Vision-Language Model for Autonomous Driving
Ruoyu Yao, Yubin Wang, Haichao Liu, Rui Yang, Zengqi Peng, Lei Zhu, Jun Ma
Decision-making and motion planning constitute critical components for ensuring the safety and efficiency of autonomous vehicles (AVs). Existing methodologies typically adopt two paradigms: decision then planning or generation then scoring. However, the former architecture often suffers from decision-planning misalignment that incurs risky situations. Meanwhile, the latter struggles to balance short-term operational metrics (e.g., immediate motion smoothness) with long-term tactical goals (e.g., route efficiency), resulting in myopic or overly conservative behaviors. To address these issues, we introduce PRIMA, a preference-informed multimodal trajectory planning framework assisted by a Vision-Language Model (VLM). Our approach employs a tri-stage cognitive decomposition protocol, encompassing scene understanding, action selection, and confidence assessment, to generate diverse candidate actions paired with verbalized confidence scores. This reasoning mechanism exposes alternative tactical choices and provides an empirical preference signal for balancing them with downstream planning quality. Furthermore, we propose a novel planning module that integrates a diffusion model for trajectory generation and a hierarchical refinement process to find the optimal trajectory. This enables the selection over trajectory candidates accounting for both low-level solution quality and high-level tactical preferences, avoiding the risks within one-shot decisions and overcoming the limitations of short-sighted scoring mechanisms. Comprehensive simulation-based closed-loop evaluations on nuPlan and InterPlan demonstrate competitive performance across common and long-tail benchmarks. A paired controlled intervention further evaluates the incremental decision utility of the verbalized confidence signal. The code will be released upon acceptance.

♻ ☆ JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
Tian Lyu, Yichen Jiang, Ziyuan Cheng, Yunda Yan, Xiangyu Pan, Junjie Jiang, Jialin Yu, Boyu Ning, Pietro Liò, Fan Mo
Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

☆ DUO Policy: Bridging Human Video Coverage and Robot Precision for Fine-Grained Manipulation
Mingxi Jia, Patton Jiyang Yin, Haojie Huang, Ivy Xiao He, Xuanru Liu, Gefei Liu, Dian Wang, Stefanie Tellex
Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. Project Webpage: https://mingxi-jia.github.io/duo_policy_site/

☆ JEPA-Tuner: From Predictive Fine-Tuning to Asynchronous Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
Jingxiang Qu, Tian Xie, Youngjin Hong, Changhyun Choi, Yang Katie Zhao, Yi Liu
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.
☆ ViewPACT: Multi-View Geometric Augmentation and Pose-Action Co-Training for Viewpoint-Robust Manipulation
Chenglang Tu, Feng Chen, Ruizhe Liu, Pei Zhou, Binbin Huang, Chen Xu, Yanchao Yang, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
Image policies are scalable but remain brittle to camera viewpoint changes. On LIBERO, we identify proprioception as an input shortcut: masking robot states sharply degrades several policies, while retraining from images alone recovers much of the loss. We introduce ViewPACT, an image policy trained with privileged geometric supervision. Auxiliary objectives recover end-effector and task-relevant object poses in the camera frame, while deployment requires only RGB observations. Joint geometric supervision improves mean simulation success from 37.4% to 78.4% under unseen external-camera viewpoints, with more modest gains under separately evaluated object, scene, and camera-intrinsic shifts. Across four real-robot tasks, combining simulated and real-image geometric supervision achieves 68.1% mean success, versus 3.1% for fixed-view behavior cloning and 30.6% for the strongest evaluated alternative. These results support geometric supervision for viewpoint robustness in the evaluated fixed-view demonstration setting.

☆ BO-COMM: Bidirectional Optical System for Simultaneous Localization and Communication in Swarm Robotics
Cheng Hu, Haotian Wu, Qi Lin, Manrui Zheng, Shigang Yue, Tao Zou, Jigen Peng
Swarm robotics experiments require observations of robot pose and operational state, together with mechanisms for returning environmental information to the robots. Shared channel wireless communication can face contention and congestion as concurrent reporting demands increase, while a static visual marker does not itself convey changing robot states. We present BO-COMM, an optical system that combines pose estimation and dynamic state reporting with optical downstream interaction. A camera observes circular LED arrays mounted on Colias IV robots with CEU-PLUS extension units.Ring-based voting estimates robot centers, and the spatial LED pattern provides orientation and an encoded state. A projector supplies spatial environmental cues, while an infrared module provides a separate command channel. Processing-time measurements, path-following and color-reporting experiments, and a multi-pheromone demonstration illustrate the operation of this architecture in a planar arena. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining optical pose and state observations with environmental feedback in the tested hardware and arena configuration.
☆ Distributed Interactive Conformal Prediction for Multi-Agent Systems
Daniel M. Cherenson, Dimitra Panagou
Multi-agent systems increasingly rely on learning-enabled components and distributed algorithms for perception, estimation, and control, introducing uncertainty that makes it challenging to satisfy mission requirements. Conformal prediction quantifies uncertainty with distribution-free guarantees, but existing methods do not address the challenging combination of dependence among robots, distributed calibration, and the distribution shift induced when calibrated uncertainty bounds modify the closed-loop system. We introduce Multi-Agent Interactive Conformal Prediction (MA-ICP), a distributed framework for computing robustness margins in heterogeneous systems to satisfy mission requirements with high probability. MA-ICP aggregates robot-level nonconformity scores, which measure errors in modeled or estimated quantities, into one mission-level score per robot class, allowing dependence among robots within each mission. Mission-level scores and quantiles are computed using neighbor-to-neighbor communication in a finite number of communication rounds. Updating the robustness margins changes robot trajectories and distributed algorithm outputs, so we use class-dependent score sensitivities to upper bound the shift in mission-level scores. We then establish calibration-conditional coverage guarantees per robot class for the updated margins. We demonstrate MA-ICP on cooperative payload control, formation control with obstacle avoidance, and distributed target tracking missions.
☆ graspit-py: A Python Interface to GraspIt! for Grasp Planning Under Pose and Friction Uncertainty SP
Clinton Enwerem, John S. Baras, Calin Belta
In simulated multifingered grasps, pose error can change contacts formed during hand closure, while friction uncertainty changes the loads supported by those contacts. Existing C++ APIs and ROS 1 services provide programmatic GraspIt! access but require native bindings or a service transport layer for Python use and application-specific integration of contact geometry with uncertainty sampling. A Python workflow for these studies must connect native closure and contacts to caller-defined wrench scores, uncertainty samples, and command reconstruction. We present graspit-py, a Python interface to native GraspIt! operations that supplies this workflow. The interface provides native scene access, contact-wrench analysis, and configurable approach planning under pose and friction uncertainty. A grasp record associates the object-relative palm pose and closed independent coordinates with nominal contacts and quality scores evaluated under sampled pose and friction conditions. Our MuJoCo exporter derives serial hinge chains and affine joint couplings, including nonzero reference angles, and preserves individual collision components. Across 75 configurations of five hand models, maximum discrepancy between source and exported palm-frame vertex sets was approximately 1.3 micrometers against a 100-micrometer geometry tolerance. We isolated reference-angle and collision-component effects through controlled ablations and validated 1,920 directional task-wrench capacity calculations against independent Cartesian-force linear programs. In a common GraspIt! workload, median reset-close-score-state cycle latency through direct Python was 10.7% lower than through persistent ROS 1 services. An executable export-plan-reconstruct workflow and grasp examples on six hand models demonstrate how the contact, score, and joint representations support numerical analysis and command reconstruction.

☆ DMPT-Swarm: A Directional Mass-Preserving Transform for Decentralized Swarm Navigation in Obstacle Environments
Jacob Lee, Samuel Sutphin, Haroon Malik, Chang Liu, Pingping Zhu
This paper presents a decentralized microscopic control framework for swarm navigation in obstacle environments, given a precomputed macroscopic trajectory represented by Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). To generate obstacle-aware reference locations without inter-agent communication, we first employ affine transport between multivariate normal (MVN) distributions under the Wasserstein-2 metric. We then propose a directional mass-preserving transform (DMPT) to incorporate obstacle effects by modifying radial transport while preserving directional structure. Based on the transformed references, a local artificial potential field (APF)-based controller is applied for navigation. Each agent operates independently, reducing communication and computational burden. Simulation results demonstrate improved efficiency and obstacle avoidance compared to conventional APF-based methods

☆ World Models for Ocean Engineering: A Critical Review of Maritime Autonomy, Adaptive Latent Prediction, Digital Twins, and Biodiversity Monitoring
Basma Dokkara, Esteban W. G. Cluab, Luiz M. G. Goncalves, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante
Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.
☆ SANA-Robot: Efficient World Action Model with Hybrid Memory
Yuyang Zhao, Zekai Li, Yicheng Pan, Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Jiaxu Xing, Moritz Reuss, Quanquan Peng, Junsong Chen, Enze Xie, Zhijian Liu, Song Han
World action models (WAMs) leverage the world knowledge of video generation models to improve action generation by aligning visual prediction with action prediction. However, their prediction overhead prevents real-time deployment on edge devices, and they usually lack an effective long-term memory. We introduce SANA-Robot, a 4.5B WAM with minute-level memory that runs in real time on edge devices, built on the following core designs: (1) hybrid memory at constant cost: our WAM relies on linear attention to maintain a global memory with a fixed-size state, and on sliding window softmax attention layers that propagate previous information, enabling high success rates on tasks requiring whole-episode memory while keeping an efficient and constant inference speed; (2) a unified model: by dynamically applying different noise levels to action and video tokens, SANA-Robot can serve not only as a policy but also as a world simulator; (3) a full-stack infrastructure for both memory training and inference, including efficient data packing and shuffling as well as memory-phase-based asynchronous execution. SANA-Robot achieves the best performance on the memory dimension of RoboDojo among models of medium size (about 5B) and the highest success rates on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro and LIBERO-Max. In real-world deployment, SANA-Robot takes 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 with FP8 GEMMs and 115 ms with NVFP4 GEMMs, and achieves closed-loop, real-time asynchronous robot control at 30 Hz on edge devices, demonstrating both the efficiency and the effectiveness of SANA-Robot. Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/Sana/Robot/
☆ T-Tac: A Soft and Thin Active Thermal Tactile Sensor for Robotic In-Grasp Material Identification
Jiankun Li, Yu Feng, Yehui Liu, Meng Chen, Rui Luo, Guanglie Zhang, Jianshu Zhou, Wen Jung Li
Accurate material identification is important for robotic manipulation, yet vision-based methods face challenges when materials have similar appearances. Herein, we report T-Tac, a soft, thin, active thermal tactile sensor that identifies materials through their transient thermal responses. T-Tac integrates a polyimide film heater with an ionic conductive film temperature sensor, providing controlled thermal excitation and resistance-based temperature measurement in a film assembly suitable for mounting on robotic grippers. Single-sided transient plane source modeling and finite element simulations relate the thermal response to material thermal properties, while calibration and repeated measurements characterize the heating and sensing performance. Loading experiments at room and elevated temperatures further characterize the sensor response under an applied force. A hybrid classification framework concatenates extracted thermal descriptors with multiscale convolutional neural network features and uses an ExtraTrees classifier for material prediction. Experiments on 12 materials achieve a mean classification accuracy of 92.69\% using a 3 s heating pulse and a 10 s observation window. These results support T-Tac as a compact approach to integrating active thermal material sensing into robotic end effectors. This work shed a light on the new approach for robotic material identification.
☆ Div3DAfford: Diverse 3D affordance grounding
Haomeng Zhang, Raymond A. Yeh
3D affordance grounding aims to localize 3D regions specified by an interaction query. Existing methods predict a single affordance mask, overlooking the inherent diversity of human-object interactions. We introduce diverse 3D affordance grounding, a new task that requires predicting multiple plausible regions for a given object and affordance query. We then propose Div3DAffordNet, a transformer-based set prediction model capable of generating diverse affordance regions. To address the scarcity of diverse 3D affordance data, we develop an automated pipeline leveraging 2D generative models and 3D reconstruction techniques to synthesize 3D affordances, followed by lightweight human verification (reducing the annotation time by 72X), yielding the Div3DAfford benchmark. Extensive experiments show Div3DAffordNet effectively captures multi-mask affordance regions. Our method achieves the SOTA affordance grounding performance in the multi-mask setting, reducing GED-SIM from 0.745 to 0.492, while maintaining competitive single-mask performance on the standard benchmark of 19.0 mIoU.
☆ NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
Ahad Jawaid, Alexander Swerdlow, Yu Xiang
Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.
☆ LIBERO-MOR: A Multimodal Robustness Benchmark Across the Vision-Language-Action Pipeline
Qihang Chen, Tengjie Li, Hongwei Lu, Jason Wu, Chyna Qu, Shikui Tu, Lei Xu
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on robot manipulation benchmarks. Translating this progress into reliable deployment calls for systematic evaluation of how policies respond to variations throughout the robot interaction loop. We introduce LIBERO-MOR, a multimodal robustness benchmark across the vision-language-action pipeline. Built on standard LIBERO, it covers five deployment-facing domains: vision, language, proprioception, action execution, and environment. The benchmark comprises 22 deployment-inspired perturbations, each evaluated at three severity levels across 40 tasks under a paired clean-perturbed protocol, enabling controlled and reproducible comparisons. We evaluate seven representative VLA models spanning diverse action-generation mechanisms. Our experiments reveal substantial robustness gaps behind high clean-task success, together with shared vulnerabilities and distinct model-specific failure patterns across domains. Severity analysis further distinguishes progressive degradation, collapse at stronger interventions, and failures triggered at the mildest tested level. By connecting aggregate performance to pipeline domains, individual perturbations, and intervention strength, LIBERO-MOR provides a systematic framework for diagnosing VLA robustness and guiding the development of more reliable robot policies.
☆ Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead for Vision-Language-Action Models
Qihang Chen, Tengjie Li, Hongwei Lu, Jason Wu, Chyna Qu, Shikui Tu, Lei Xu
Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over in both simulation and real-robot settings.

Yitong Hong, Xiangdong Feng, Xiaoxi Sun, Senqiao Yang, Boyao Han, Zhejian Yang, Shiyang Zhou, Yongcai Wang, Pengguang Chen, Shu Liu, Li Jiang, Zhuotao Tian
Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the $[15,21]$ switching range, CAS improves $π_{0.5}$ from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. Code will be made publicly available.

Feiyang Jia, Lin Liu, Zhicheng Bao, Caiyan Jia, Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Lina Han, Yan Zhao, Xiaoshuai Hao
World models hold great promise for autonomous driving planning, yet their ability to imagine the future often comes at a formidable computational cost. Efficiency efforts, such as knowledge distillation and domain-specific pre-training, often shift this burden to costly teachers or training pipelines, leaving lightweight world modeling an open challenge. We introduce FastWorld, a natively lightweight world-model framework for efficient autonomous driving planning. FastWorld reduces computation through compact scene representations, short-horizon action-conditioned prediction, and selective candidate verification and score refinement. On NAVSIMv1, FastWorld achieves 92.2 PDMS at 132 FPS on a single 4090 GPU. It also achieves 89.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2 and an average L2 of 0.40 over 3 seconds at 17 FPS on nuScenes. ☆ VTLA-RL: Learning Visuotactile Policies for Load-Adaptive Grasping
Qiwei Wu, Qixuan Li, Xin Xiang, Xiangyu Chen, Xiang Xiao, Daochen Shi, Ruihua Zhang, Renjing Xu
Vision-language-action foundation models learn general manipulation priors, but object mass and local slip are difficult to infer from vision alone. Changing loads require contact-driven grasp adjustments that demonstrations collected under fixed conditions may not adequately cover. We present VTLA-RL to study visuotactile grasping policies and their reinforcement learning (RL) post-training under varying loads. Our main approach shares a visual encoder between tactile-image histories and RGB inputs to jointly generate and execute motion and bilateral force targets in a unified action space. Mixed real and simulated demonstrations first establish motion and contact priors. Two-stage multi-task RL then uses only simulated interaction to optimize the policy through task-success returns without continued real-demonstration supervision, and the trained policy deploys directly to real robots. We compare tactile representations and RL post-training routes in simulation and separately evaluate load variation and placement perturbations on hardware. The full method achieves higher grasping success than the supervised initialization, while RL post-training gains differ across approaches, providing empirical evidence for choosing representations and training approaches for this task.
☆ Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts

In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools.

☆ Data-Driven Trajectory Prediction via Probabilistic Modes and Constrained Optimization
Danyang Li, Ana Theodora Balaci, Matthew Cleaveland, Roberto Tron
Predicting the future trajectories of surrounding agents is a fundamental requirement for safe autonomous driving. Since agent intent is inherently uncertain, multimodal prediction is essential to account for the full range of plausible future behaviors. We introduce Probabilistic Modes and Constrained Optimization trajectory prediction (ProMo-CoOp), a two-stage data-driven framework. At design time, trajectories are clustered into behavioral modes and a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) provides probabilistic mode assignments. At prediction time, a candidate trajectory is generated for each mode by solving a convex optimization problem that enforces consistency with the observed trajectory and uses the precomputed mode assignments to guide prediction toward the selected behavioral mode. The framework also supports Signal Temporal Logic (STL)-derived behavioral constraints, with predicate satisfaction probabilities estimated using Conditional Flow Matching (CFM). Experiments show that ProMo-CoOp outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, and that STL-based constraints can further improve performance when the predicted predicate satisfactions are reliable.
☆ IRIS: Inverse Dynamics from Random Exploration with Eye-in-hand Sensing
Xiaoxiong Zhang, Zhiqiang Zhou, Tze Ho Elden Tse, Linfang Zheng, Wei Zhang
Imagine-then-execute methods offer a promising paradigm for video-based manipulation, where a video planner predicts future visual subgoals and an inverse dynamics model (IDM) grounds them into robot actions. Despite their promise, these methods remain limited by action grounding. First, the IDM is typically trained on limited task-specific demonstrations and can generalize poorly even when given oracle visual subgoals, indicating that action grounding remains a bottleneck beyond visual planning errors. Second, precise execution benefits from eye-in-hand observations, but eye-in-hand video planning is both hard to learn and hard to scale: the viewpoint moves with the robot, and such videos are scarce at internet scale. To overcome these challenges, we propose IRIS, a video-based manipulation framework that learns a highly generalizable, execution-aware IDM. First, IRIS scales action grounding by pretraining the IDM on task-agnostic random exploration data, which provides diverse visual state transitions paired with robot actions without human task annotation. Second, it extends the IDM with eye-in-hand sensing through a two-stage training scheme, without requiring eye-in-hand video planning. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show that IRIS improves action grounding and data efficiency, enables more precise execution, and achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art manipulation policies.
☆ Distilling Touch into Vision-Only Policies for Contact-Rich Manipulation
Chen Yang, Linhao Wang, Linzhe Shi, Guohui Zhang, Changjie Wu, Hang Zhang, Haoyu Li, Mu Xu, Jiansheng Fan, Chen Wang
Tactile feedback benefits contact-rich manipulation, yet deploying tactile sensors introduces additional hardware and maintenance requirements. Tactile experience can still provide effective supervision for policies that operate without tactile sensors at deployment. Tactile imagination methods such as TacImag remove this hardware dependency by predicting tactile observations, but retain a reconstruction stage whose errors can propagate into action generation. We present TacitTouch, a distillation framework that transfers tactile-guided behavior directly into a vision-only policy. The core shift is from "learn to imagine what touch would feel like" to "learn to behave as if you could feel touch": the student directly learns tactile-guided action patterns without reconstructing tactile observations. A frozen visuotactile teacher supervises the student's denoising predictions and intermediate action representations at the same noisy action and flow time. Training also uses demonstrated-action supervision. Deployment retains only the visual policy, with no tactile encoder, expert, or generator. Across four simulated UniVTAC tasks and four real-world tasks, TacitTouch achieves absolute improvements of 16.0% and 22.5% in mean success rate over vision-only control, respectively. The absolute gaps to the teacher using measured tactile input are only 2.0% and 3.75%, respectively. In robustness tests, it also outperforms TacImag, with absolute gains of up to 20.0% in mean success rate. Project page: https://pier-lab.github.io/tacittouch/

☆ Doing More with Less: Complex Manipulation with a Contact-Adaptive Robotic Hand
Hyung Gon Shin, Sanghoon Jung
Anthropomorphic robotic hands offer the potential to manipulate objects designed for human hands in environments adapted to human use. However, developing a robotic hand that replicates the human hand in terms of morphology, degrees of freedom, force output, durability, and sensing capabilities remains a formidable challenge, as these requirements inherently involve trade-offs. Here, we propose a robotic hand mechanism designed to address several of these trade-offs by enabling contact-adaptive finger motion, slender fingers, a wide grasping range, and sustained gripping force. We also introduce a motion glove based on quaternion swing-twist decomposition to extract human manipulation intentions and translate them into robotic hand commands, along with a forearm-mounted interface designed to enhance the operator's sense of embodiment. Experimental demonstrations show that a robotic hand with limited active degrees of freedom and no tactile sensing can perform complex tasks, including smartphone pickup and charging, in-hand manipulation, object unboxing and repackaging, and cutting and tying cords, through the combination of the proposed mechanism and effective bimanual coordination.

☆ Fast World Planner: Advantage-Aware Action-Chunk Policy for Online Planning
Jiangtao Kong, Yuchen Wang, Yandong Luo, Rongchao Xu, Guang Wang, Yanbing Mao, Lu Gan, Tianyi Zhou, Huajie Shao
Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete $H$-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete $H$-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)
☆ AsyncMixVLA: Runtime Asynchronous Robot Policy Switching for Adaptation to Dynamic Environments SC
Tamoghno Das, Keyon Jazayeri, Yerin Cho, Nazmul Takbir, Arshia Aravinthan, Nikil Dutt
Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.
comment: Manuscript prepared for the DAC 2027 Research Track (IEEE conference format)
☆ Selective ROM Weight Storage for Responsive LLM Control on Edge Robots
Boxiang Song, Zhihong Chen, Xiaoyu Hao, Jinhong Huang, Chengkai Zhu, Jiaqi Yang, Hongyang Pan, Changhao Yan, Keren Zhu
Edge robots increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for complex tasks, demanding efficient inference alongside timely control. Limited memory capacity constrains model deployment, while repeated weight transfers during decoding compete with activations and KV cache for external bandwidth. Sequential generation of robot actions further delays decisions and periodic control on shared hardware. We present a hybrid memory architecture with heterogeneous scheduling to address these bottlenecks jointly. Banked ROM stores selected fixed weights and supplies a standard compute array through a dedicated datapath. LPDDR retains the remaining weights and mutable state, preserving model flexibility. Coordinated operand delivery and preemption at output slice boundaries accelerate inference while limiting interference with periodic control. A structured decision interface scores candidate phases in a single forward pass, avoiding sequential token generation for routine choices. Together, these mechanisms improve memory service, compute access, and decision execution for edge robotic workloads. Experiments with Qwen3-8B achieve a peak decode speedup of 1.56$\times$ and reduce P99 task response time by a factor of approximately 227.27$\times$, while completing 100.00\% of the tested grasping and transport tasks.
☆ PhysPPF: Learning Robotic Manipulation with Past, Present, and Future Physical Representations
Junjie Li, Dawei Yan, Guoting Wei, Ruike Song, Lu Wang, Qingguo Chen, Zhenbo Luo, Haokui Zhang, Chunhua Shen
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation, yet complex tasks requiring both precise 3D contact and long-horizon coordination remain challenging. Most existing studies enhance spatial perception or temporal reasoning in VLAs separately. Spatial methods primarily inject geometric or affordance priors into current-frame perception without tracking multi-step transitions, while history-aware and world-model VLAs typically capture past context or future dynamics in 2D feature or pixel spaces, either lacking explicit 3D contact cues or incurring high generation overhead. To address this, we propose PhysPPF, a VLA framework that performs unified spatiotemporal modeling in a compact physical token space. Spatially, WWH (What-Where-How) distills pretrained perception teachers exclusively during training into compact token groups capturing what 3D structures occupy the scene, where to interact, and how the gripper should approach, without test-time 3D encoders. Temporally, operating directly in this WWH space without pixel reconstruction, PPF (Past-Present-Future) consolidates executed states into a bounded past physical memory and jointly infers present and future physical tokens via an asymmetric world model. Parallel gated branches then inject these past, present, and future representations into a flow-matching action expert to guide manipulation without cross-temporal interference. Extensive experiments on SimplerEnv, CALVIN, and LIBERO show that PhysPPF consistently outperforms existing spatial, history-aware, and world-model VLAs with modest latency and parameter overhead, improving over the StarVLA baseline by +17.2 points on SimplerEnv, +29.3 points on CALVIN, and +3.5 points on LIBERO.

☆ SBTenv: A Literature-Validated Split-Belt Treadmill Simulation Environment
Philip Byrne, John Drazan, Nidhi Seethapathi
The split-belt treadmill is an important tool for studying human locomotor adaptation. Physics-based simulations complement such experiments by allowing hypotheses about the mechanisms of adaptation to be tested directly, and high-throughput simulation is increasingly needed as these models grow in complexity. However, no open-source split-belt treadmill environment exists in MuJoCo, a physics engine widely used for high-throughput simulation. Here, we present SBTenv, a split-belt treadmill environment built in MuJoCo and validated against published experimental data from a rimless wheel walking passively on a split-belt treadmill. By modeling compliant contacts at the spoke tips, SBTenv reproduces the experimental average steady velocity ($R^2=0.643$, RMSE $=0.0162$ m/s) without the empirical geometric correction required in prior simulations. We expect SBTenv, openly shared, to enable high-throughput simulation of musculoskeletal and robotic locomotion on a split-belt treadmill.

☆ Environment-Aware Probabilistic State Estimation of Continuum Robots from Planar Imaging
Aedan Mangan, Spencer Teetaert, Chengnan Shentu, Michael G. Brandel, Jeremy J. Heit, Alexander Norbash, Timothy D. Barfoot, Nikolay Atanasov, Tania K. Morimoto, Jessica Burgner-Kahrs
Continuum robots are compliant along their entire length, making them well suited to navigating confined environments where contact with surrounding structures is often unavoidable. However, this compliance makes their modeling more complex compared to rigid robots, especially under contact, so their state must often be estimated from information available during operation. In many applications, the environment is known in advance, for example from preoperative imaging in medicine or from design models in industrial inspection. We present a probabilistic state estimator that represents the known environment as a signed distance field, informing the estimated shape. Continuous in arclength and time, it estimates the full state from asynchronous measurements anywhere along the robot. It also fuses planar images of body-fixed markers from a moving camera with commanded actuation, so the robot needs no embedded sensors. In a simulated aortic arch and a hardware phantom, the estimator tracked the robot into the target branch, and with a single view, using the known environment lowered the tip error from 2.5% to 1.6% and from 20.0% to 11.3% of the robot length, respectively. The continuous estimate of the full state and its uncertainty can support navigation and control of sensorless continuum robots.

☆ Lifted Multiple Shooting for Parallel-in-Time Contact-Rich Trajectory Optimization
Wei-Chen Li, Glen Chou
Planning through contact requires accounting for the coupled dynamics of a robot and its environment, including inertial effects, contact forces, and friction. However, the non-smoothness and multimodality of contact dynamics and contact geometry makes gradient-based optimization challenging. In this work, we propose lifted multiple shooting, a trajectory optimization transcription that can be solved directly using nonlinear program solvers. By introducing contact impulses as optimization variables, our formulation allows the optimizer to satisfy the state-transition constraints using friction-cone-feasible impulses while separately enforcing their consistency with the contact model. Our formulation supports a broad class of contact constitutive relations, with sensitivities computed through implicit differentiation. To enable efficient planning over long horizons and for high-dimensional systems, we further introduce IP-PAS, a parallel-in-time primal-dual interior-point solver that achieves O(log T) parallel computational depth. We evaluate the proposed methods on six fully dynamic contact-rich planning tasks, including nonprehensile pushing and in-hand manipulation, without contact-guiding costs. Lifted multiple shooting improves success rates by up to 81.5 percentage points over standard multiple shooting, while IP-PAS achieves solution quality comparable to serial methods with up to a 3.1x speedup and scales to horizons of 40,000 timesteps.
☆ AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Weisong Shi
Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.
☆ Real-time Priority-aware UAS Arrival Planning Framework for Multi-layer UTM SP
Anisha Mohapatra, Prasanna Ramamurthy, Shridhar Velhal, M. Sethumadhavan, Suresh Sundaram
This paper proposes a real-time, priority-aware UAS arrival-planning framework for multi-layer UTM terminal airspace represented as a funnel of concentric rings, discrete holding slots, connecting edges, and a landing pad. Managing dense arrivals is challenging because terminal resources are limited and UAS must remain spatially and temporally separated throughout their approaches. New arrivals, wind disturbances, and emergency landing requests further require rapid replanning beyond conventional landing-pad sequencing. To achieve computational tractability, the framework employs a greedy planning method that first establishes a priority-aware landing order and then plans the UAS sequentially. For each UAS, the method determines its slot assignments, traversal path, landing time, and slot entry and exit times while treating previously planned trajectories as fixed. Spatial and temporal constraints prevent conflicts on holding slots, connecting edges, and the landing pad. Within a rolling-horizon implementation, the framework incorporates new arrivals, reactively adjusts plans affected by wind disturbances, and prioritizes emergency UAS without altering completed operations. Computational results show that the method generates and updates feasible, conflict-free arrival plans within operational time limits while providing expedited landing access to emergency UAS. The results demonstrate the suitability of the proposed framework for responsive and safety-critical arrival management in dynamic multi-layer UTM environments. Video link: https://youtu.be/F9IP1dz-9PE

☆ LoKiTO: Local Kinodynamic Trajectory Optimization for UAVs based on Memory-Efficient Neural Distance Fields
Guillermo Gil-Garcia, J. A. Cobano, L. Merino, F. Caballero
This paper introduces LoKiTO, a 3D local kinodynamic trajectory optimizer that combines a Chebyshev polynomial parameterization with an online neural Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) representation for aerial robotics. While current gradient-based planners often struggle with the high memory requirements of explicit volumetric maps or fail to strictly enforce dynamic limits, LoKiTO embeds kinodynamic constraints directly into a modular cost function and exploits the numerical conditioning properties of the Chebyshev basis. Collision awareness is provided by a continuous, memory-efficient neural ESDF updated online from LiDAR measurements, which drastically reduces map memory consumption to approximately 1.0 MB. Benchmarking in highly cluttered simulated environments against state-of-the-art baselines (Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner) demonstrates the superiority of our approach. Experimental results show that LoKiTO achieves over 99.4% dynamic feasibility compliance, significantly outperforming the baselines, and maintaining higher median clearance from obstacles. By coupling a well-conditioned continuous parameterization with explicit kinodynamic reasoning, LoKiTO provides a practical and extensible basis for local replanning in aerial robotics.

♻ ☆ Teleoperator-Aware and CBF-Based Adaptive Nonlinear MPC for Shared Autonomy in Obstacle Avoidance of Legged Robots
Ruturaj Sambhus, Muneeb Ahmad, Basit Muhammad Imran, Sujith Vijayan, Dylan P. Losey, Kaveh Akbari Hamed
Safe and effective collaboration between humans and autonomous legged robots is a fundamental challenge in shared autonomy, particularly for teleoperated systems navigating cluttered environments. Shared autonomy for legged robots remains challenging due to uncertain human commands, collision-avoidance requirements, and the need to coordinate high-level planning with dynamically feasible locomotion. This paper presents a teleoperator-aware, control barrier function (CBF)-based, adaptive nonlinear model predictive control (ANMPC) framework for shared autonomy of quadrupedal robots in obstacle-avoidance tasks. The framework employs a prescribed arbitration weight between human and robot actions while modeling human inputs using a noisily rational Boltzmann model, whose parameters are adapted online through a projected gradient descent (PGD) law based on observed joystick commands. CBF constraints are incorporated into a computationally efficient NMPC formulation to promote obstacle avoidance while accounting for predicted human actions. The hierarchical architecture integrates high-level CBF-based ANMPC (10 Hz), mid-level dynamics-aware NMPC (60 Hz) enforcing single rigid body (SRB) dynamics, and low-level nonlinear whole-body control (500 Hz). Human-in-the-loop hardware experiments with ten participants on a Unitree Go2 quadruped demonstrate real-time feasibility and collision-free navigation across 50 trials. Shared autonomy reduced average human control effort by 51% and joystick activity from 88% to 42% of trial time, with comparable obstacle clearance and significantly higher perceived assistance than manual operation. Simulation-based ablation studies demonstrate improved obstacle clearance across operator rationality levels and up to a 66% reduction in median human-action prediction error through online adaptation.
♻ ☆ LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
Anh Dao, Xinxin Liu, Hang Yu, Jeffrey A Chan Santiago, Yuzhang Shang
World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.
♻ ☆ Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filtering for Data-Efficient Joint Tracking and Classification SP
Jiho Lee, Nisar R. Ahmed, Rebecca Russell
Kalman filtering performance is highly sensitive to model mismatch and noise covariance tuning. Classical adaptive filtering methods address these issues by estimating model parameters or noise covariances from measurement data but rely on a predefined model structure. Learning-based methods provide greater flexibility but typically require large supervised datasets and often lack well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. This article proposes a self-supervised Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filter (HAKF) that learns time-varying corrections to the system dynamics and process-noise covariance directly from measurements while jointly estimating the measurement-noise covariance. Because these corrections are learned from measurements alone, we analyze the structural identifiability of the corresponding time-invariant parameterizations. For a constant-velocity model with position-only measurements, an unrestricted process-noise covariance is not identifiable even when the dynamics are known, whereas a physically structured parameterization that couples the dynamics and process covariance is jointly identifiable with the measurement-noise covariance. This analysis motivates a structured HAKF variant, compared with a flexible variant that adapts the dynamics and process covariance independently. The innovation likelihood of HAKF also enables model classification through generalized Bayesian inference. In Isaac Lab simulations, the structured HAKF improves tracking accuracy over a fitted Kalman filter across all training-set sizes. When training data are limited, its advantage over the flexible variant is largest, and it outperforms a supervised recurrent neural network in both tracking and classification. On recorded DPJAIT flight trajectories, it achieves the best tracking and classification performance with near-consistent state covariance, whereas the flexible variant becomes overconfident.

♻ ☆ RecallFlow: Episodic Memory as the Source Distribution of Generative Robot Policies
Xuji Zhang, Qilin Zhong, Zichen Zhang, Wei Zhai, Jian Di, Kun Li, Yang Cao, Wenjun Lv
Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables. Project page: https://xujizhang.github.io/RecallFlow/
♻ ☆ Learning optimal gaits and styles for terrain-adaptive quadruped locomotion
Guillaume Bellegarda, Auke Ijspeert
Animals use many different gaits to locomote at different speeds across varying terrains. A longstanding question in biology and robotics is: which gait is best? This question is most often addressed from an energy-efficiency perspective on flat terrain, leaving open how the answer depends on terrain and on the criterion optimized. Here we show that gait optimality is determined jointly by terrain, performance metric, and velocity. We use deep reinforcement learning and networks of abstract oscillators, modeling spinal central pattern generators, to learn 11 quadrupedal gaits across diverse challenging terrains, together with the locomotion style (base height, foot ground clearance, foot offsets) that each requires. A second policy then selects among them to optimize a user-specified criterion such as cost of transport, base stability, or joint smoothness. Across these performance metrics and within this repertoire, every gait is optimal under at least one terrain-metric-velocity combination. The framework adapts zero-shot to gait couplings and styles never seen during training, to terrains far beyond the training distribution, and to larger quadrupeds five times the training mass. With a single additional pitch-tracking reward term, the same gait couplings also support bipedal-mode locomotion. Our method provides a general and systematic way to produce expressive locomotion and to select the gait best suited to a given terrain and criterion. Project page: https://guillaume10.github.io/terrain-gaits.
♻ ☆ Rethinking Actions: Continuity-Aware Priors for World-Model Planning
Shaobo Yang, Zichen Ai, Ziyang Ma, Qian Yang, Bin Fang
Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal. Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with the GP residual using expert future actions. The resulting planner achieves 87.07\% macro success across five simulated tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with 71.03\% for INTACT, 61.66\% for PRISM, and 58.66\% for LeWM. Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.
♻ ☆ Injecting Hallucinations in Autonomous Vehicles: A Component-Agnostic Safety Evaluation Framework
Alexandre Moreira Nascimento, Gabriel Kenji Godoy Shimanuki, Lúcio Flavio Vismari, João Batista Camargo, Jorge Rady de Almeida, Paulo Sergio Cugnasca, Anna Carolina Muller Queiroz, Jeremy Noah Bailenson
Perception failures in autonomous vehicles (AV) remain a major safety concern because they can directly compromise decision-making and contribute to unsafe behavior. To study how these failures affect safety, researchers typically inject artificial faults into real-world or simulated components and observe the resulting outcomes. However, existing fault injection (FI) studies often target a single sensor within the machine perception (MP) module, resulting in siloed frameworks that are difficult to generalize or integrate into unified simulation environments. This work addresses that limitation by reframing perception failures as hallucinations, that is, false perceptions that distort an AV's situational awareness and may trigger unsafe control actions. Building on this concept, we propose a configurable, component-agnostic hallucination injection framework that induces six plausible hallucination types in an open-source simulation environment. A total of 18,356 simulations (8,695 baseline and 9,661 with hallucinations injected) were executed while AVs crossed an unsignalized intersection with transversal traffic. The results statistically validate the framework and quantify the impact of each hallucination type on collisions and on the minimum distance between the AV and the nearest vehicle, used as a continuous proxy for the safety margin. Certain hallucinations, especially missed detection, blind region, angular drift, phantom perception, and latency, significantly increase the odds of collision, while linear drift significantly reduces minimum distances without producing a statistically significant increase in collision odds in the evaluated scenario. The proposed framework provides a scalable and statistically grounded method for evaluating AV safety under perception distortions and supports future research on fault tolerance and resilient AV design.
comment: 28 pages, 16 figures, 27 tables. Accepted for publication in IEEE Access
♻ ☆ U-ViLAR: Uncertainty-Aware Visual Localization for Autonomous Driving via Differentiable Association and Registration
Xiaofan Li, Zhihao Xu, Chenming Wu, Zhao Yang, Yumeng Zhang, Jiang-Jiang Liu, Haibao Yu, Fan Duan, Xiaoqing Ye, Yuan Wang, Shirui Li, Xun Sun, Ji Wan, Jun Wang
Accurate localization using visual information is a critical yet challenging task, especially in urban environments where nearby buildings and construction sites significantly degrade GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) signal quality. This issue underscores the importance of visual localization techniques in scenarios where GNSS signals are unreliable. This paper proposes U-ViLAR, a novel uncertainty-aware visual localization framework designed to address these challenges while enabling adaptive localization using high-definition (HD) maps or navigation maps. Specifically, our method first extracts features from the input visual data and maps them into Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) space to enhance spatial consistency with the map input. Subsequently, we introduce: a) Perceptual Uncertainty-guided Association, which mitigates errors caused by perception uncertainty, and b) Localization Uncertainty-guided Registration, which reduces errors introduced by localization uncertainty. By effectively balancing the coarse-grained large-scale localization capability of association with the fine-grained precise localization capability of registration, our approach achieves robust and accurate localization. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple localization tasks. Furthermore, our model has undergone rigorous testing on large-scale autonomous driving fleets and has demonstrated stable performance in various challenging urban scenarios.

♻ ☆ DriveAnchor: Progressive Anchor-based Flow Learning for Autonomous Driving Planning
Limin Yan, Haoyun Tang, Yutao Qiu, Hongqing Liu, Zhandong Mei, Haoyu Xu
Autonomous-driving planners must generate route- and maneuver-compliant trajectories under a limited decoder-call budget while adapting offline to black-box static-collision feedback. We propose DriveAnchor, a three-stage framework built around a shared vocabulary of recorded trajectories and a continuous trajectory interface. The vocabulary supports flow-matching (FM) residual learning, Energy Field (EF) corridor-conditioned initialization, and anchor-guided zeroth-order reward fine-tuning. The reward update operates in trajectory space without policy likelihoods or reward gradients, enabling offline adaptation of a deterministic decoder. On sampled nuPlan scenarios, EF guidance and reward fine-tuning each improve the mean closed-loop score. On the same cases, the official pretrained Diffusion Planner scores higher with our reward update than with supervised fine-tuning. We further integrate the trajectory generator into a real vehicle's planning pipeline and demonstrate its operation on urban roads. On 10,000 held-out internal scenarios, under the original non-EF prior and a fixed two-call FM budget, reward fine-tuning reduces short- and long-horizon static candidate collision rates from 27.22% and 56.54% to 2.94% and 7.15%, respectively, and improves 8-s best-of-set minADE from 2.27 to 1.34 m. In a separate junction diagnostic on checkpoints before Stage 3, one and two EF calls raise corridor-guidance satisfaction from 22.10% to 74.13% and 87.92%, respectively. Additional ablations support the vocabulary size and the anchor-guided sampling configuration. On NVIDIA Drive Orin, two EF calls and two FM calls take 2.06 ms per scene on average. Code and deployment videos are available on the project page: https://driveanchor-meituan.github.io/

♻ ☆ TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
Weile Li, Yunfan Lou, Muqing Shi, Zihao Zhang, Zhenbiao Huang, Boxian Yao, Xiyu Zhu, Zhibo Pang
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://tacinno.github.io
♻ ☆ ThinkWAM: Rethinking Latent Futures for Action Refinement
Haoyun Tang, Baqiao Deng, Enjin Zhou, Songwen Tian, Keyao Xu, Bowen Jing, Kun Wang, Ke Ma, Zhandong Mei, Huibin Li
World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk is identical for every proposal and thus carries no proposal-specific signal, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.

♻ ☆ Visual Foresight for Agentic Reasoning Before Action in Urban Navigation
Jing Xie, Shouwei Ruan, Yubin Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Junwei Yang, Songchang Jin, Dianxi Shi
Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of action consequences, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, a training-free agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with visual foresight for reasoning before action. Our central idea is to use predicted future views to assess proposed actions in the context of persistent medium-horizon subgoals and observed experience. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. To enable visual foresight, a predictive world sandbox uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to generate future views of proposed movements, providing visual cues for reasoning about their consequences beyond the current observation. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions using the subgoal and accumulated experience to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
♻ ☆ RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation SC
Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Yida Yang, Lei Qian, Zhaoye Zhou, Hongru Zhang, Kai Ye, Shuyuan Hu, Yiran Mao, Zewei Ye, Bo Zhao
Evaluating embodied-AI policies in closed loop across simulation benchmarks such as LIBERO and RoboTwin requires repeated integration, as each benchmark defines its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention. Evaluation can also be slow: with a StarVLA checkpoint, the 5,000 episodes of RoboTwin Easy take 17.5 hours on four RTX PRO 5000 GPUs. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluators identifies two bottlenecks: alternating between one simulator and inference leaves the GPU at only 14.3% average utilization on LIBERO-Long, while rendering at every control step on RoboTwin means an action-chunk policy reads only one of every 16 rendered observations. We present RoboScope Kit, an evaluation toolkit that integrates each model and benchmark once through a unified interface, keeping each benchmark's native evaluator and scoring, and accelerates evaluation through two mechanisms. (1) Scheduling: simulator workers and policy replicas scale independently, with autotuning sizing both pools to each workload and host. (2) Runtime optimization: the simulation runtime skips unconsumed simulation and rendering work without changing the policy's inputs or outcomes. On a single RTX 4090, RoboScope Kit runs LIBERO-Long 6.2$\times$ faster and 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes 13.2$\times$ faster than StarVLA, and 2.1-7.3$\times$ faster than RLinf and vla-eval. Scaling to four RTX PRO 5000 GPUs, it evaluates all 5,000 RoboTwin Easy episodes in 66 minutes (15.8$\times$ faster). LIBERO-Long success rates stay within 0.3 percentage points of StarVLA, and every RoboTwin episode matches its exact outcome and terminal step.
